newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia grain market murky, needs imports-newspaper.
newsitem.headline: Russia grain market murky, needs imports-newspaper.

text.p: Skewed data, high domestic prices and peasant hoarding are obscuring Russia's grain import needs, the Sevodnya newspaper said on Tuesday.
But Russia would still need to buy from abroad in 1997, the daily said.
"Not even Alexander Zaveryukha knows how much grain is in the country," it said, adding, "Once again, we won't get by without foreign imports".
Russia's net grain harvest in 1996 was officially 69.3 million tonnes, the second poor result in a row and one of the worst in three decades.
But Sevodnya said the real number may be higher or lower.

"Even the sector's leaders -- Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Zaveryukha and Agriculture Minister Viktor Khlystun -- who, it would seem, must know almost everything about Russian agriculture, suggest that last year's harvest was from 65-75 million tonnes and don't calculate exact data," the paper said.

"The government had already practically rejected centralised purchases last year," it said, adding later, "It's not hard to suppose that trading firms will give their preferences to foreign products."
The government said last year that it had quit the grain import business for good and that private traders would have to take the reins.
Sevodnya said Russian oil companies would import 3-4 million tonnes of grain from Kazakhstan this year.
The Economy Ministry was quoted as saying Russia's annual grain demand was 98 million tonnes and that the country could fall 20 million tonnes short this year.

Farmers, seeking to avoid taxes on their production and hoping for bigger state handouts for the next harvest, could be hiding up to two million tonnes of grain. That grain might never reach the market even though domestic prices of $200 per tonne are well above world prices, Sevodnya said.

"Against the backdrop of all of this, the Russian grain market continues to be considered one of the more attractive ones for commercial activity. How otherwise would you explain the fact that oil companies have gotten into the market?"

State financing of the sector -- where output is down one third since market reforms began in 1992 -- has fallen to 3.3 percent of federal budget expenditures from 19.0 percent in 1991, Interfax news agency quoted Agriculture Ministry documents as saying on Tuesday.
Only 57 percent of funds allocated last year for farmers were actually released, leading 1996's total agricultural output to slip seven percent on 1995 level.
